answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: This line is spoken by Jane Eyre to Mr. Rochester in Chapter 23 of Charlotte Brontë’s novel Jane Eyre (1847), and the exact wording is confirmed against the original text.

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: “I am no bird; and no net ensnares me: I am a free human being with an independent will, which I now exert to leave you.”
trail: The full scene appears in Chapter XXIII of Jane Eyre, viewable at Wikisource ↗, which reproduces the exact line.
The novel was first published on 19 October 1847 by Smith, Elder & Co., per History.com’s ‘This Day in History’ ↗.
Wikiquote's Jane Eyre page ↗ lists this line among the novel's genuine, sourced dialogue, with no misattribution flag attached.
source.excerptNote: Spoken just after Rochester compares Jane's struggle to a wild bird tearing its own plumage in desperation.
source.rightsNote: Jane Eyre was first published in 1847, well over a century ago, so the novel's text has long been in the public domain in the United States.

author.name: Charlotte Brontë
author.heading: About Charlotte Brontë
author.bio: Charlotte Brontë was the eldest of the three literary Brontë sisters and the author of Jane Eyre (1847), Shirley (1849), and Villette (1853). She first published under the male pseudonym “Currer Bell” and is credited with pioneering a bold first-person female voice in the English novel.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The line comes at the emotional peak of Chapter 23, just after Mr. Rochester has proposed marriage while Jane believes he intends to wed the wealthy Blanche Ingram. He compares her inner struggle to a wild bird tearing at its own plumage and tells her to be still — and Jane answers with this declaration of her own will.
It has since become one of the most quoted passages in Jane Eyre, often cited as an early literary statement of female independence within a Victorian courtship plot.
